CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer with recent redness and drainage.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gregory presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on his right foot that he has had for approximately two months. He reports that the ulcer recently became red and started draining, which prompted his visit. He believes he acquired the injury from walking barefoot at Dewey Beach. He describes the pain as intermittent throbbing without specific localization. He expresses particular concern about the recent onset of drainage and redness. He was previously seen by his PCP who prescribed antibiotics, but he has not yet filled the prescription and cannot recall the specific medication name, though he notes he had taken it before.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies specific pain but reports intermittent throbbing in the foot. He notes redness and drainage from the ulcer as new symptoms.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Diabetes mellitus.

MEDICATIONS
Patient reports taking diabetes medication but does not check his blood sugar regularly. Has not yet filled the antibiotic prescription from his PCP.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient walks barefoot on beaches. Recently visited Dewey Beach where he sustained the foot injury.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs normal, no fever. Right foot exam reveals a 1 by 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Wound shows redness, drainage present, and edema around the area. No necrosis, odor, or bony exposure appreciated. Patient reports increased pressure sensation but denies distinct pain with palpation.

RESULTS
X-ray of right foot: No evidence of osteomyelitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diabetic foot ulcer with infection of the skin. Patient has poorly controlled diabetes with last A1C around 10. Plan includes: (1) Order ankle brachial index (ABI) to assess blood supply to foot; (2) Perform wound debridement to remove dead tissue; (3) Prescribe clindamycin 400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days to treat infection; (4) Provide surgical shoe to reduce pressure on foot and prevent further irritation, to be worn for one month; (5) Follow-up appointment in two weeks for reassessment and possible additional debridement; (6) Reinforce need for patient to return to PCP to improve diabetes control; (7) Advise patient to call office if any issues arise between visits, and to seek urgent care or ER if fever develops or other emergencies occur.
